title: Search Models and Querying
readerIntent: Understand how Nodics exposes searchable business data without coupling callers to one search engine.
priorKnowledge: Understand the purpose of a Nodics schema and item model.
summary: Search models describe searchable behavior and normalized operations; configured providers execute engine-specific indexing and queries.

sections.heading: What is Search Models and Querying?
paragraphs: A search model is a structured request that describes filters, sorting, paging, projection, and related query choices. It separates what a caller wants to find from the database or search provider that executes the query.
Think of an advanced library request form: the reader describes subject, date, order, and result size, while the library decides how to locate the matching records safely.

sections.heading: Four different responsibilities
items: The owning business schema defines authoritative records and business rules.
A source-owned index definition declares what should be searchable.
The provider-neutral search model exposes normalized index and query operations.
A configured engine adapter translates those operations to an external engine.

sections.heading: Why this separation matters
paragraphs: Business modules should not contain Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, or Solr client calls. They declare searchable intent and call the shared search contract, allowing the engine to change without rewriting business callers.

sections.heading: Search model versus search engine
paragraphs: A search model is the Nodics contract describing searchable fields, index ownership, normalized operations, and business context. A provider translates that contract to an engine such as Elasticsearch.
Business modules depend on normalized search, not engine clients. This permits provider changes and keeps engine settings out of business schemas.

sections.heading: Search is a projection
paragraphs: The item model and owning service remain the source of truth. A search index is a rebuildable projection optimized for discovery.
Search results preserve tenant, ownership, permission, catalog, and business scopes. A fast query is not acceptable if it reveals a record the owning API would reject.

sections.heading: Normalized responsibilities
items: Create or update an index from the effective search model.
Index, update, or remove documents after authoritative changes.
Execute supported text, filter, sort, aggregation, pagination, and identifier queries.
Rebuild or reconcile indexes after imports, migrations, mapping changes, or drift.
Report provider health, index state, failures, lag, and diagnostics.

sections.heading: Example: find enterprises
paragraphs: An employee searches Enterprise by code, description, or approved aliases. The query resolves tenant and authorization context, selects the Enterprise search model, and executes through the configured provider.
Results expose safe display fields. Selecting one retrieves or mutates it through the Profile API; Axis never treats a search document as update authority.

sections.heading: Consistency and implementation choices
items: Synchronous indexing reduces read-after-write delay but adds provider latency to mutations.
Asynchronous indexing isolates writes but introduces lag, retry, and reconciliation.
Bulk import coordinates indexing and exposes finalization status.
Delete, publishing, tenant movement, and schema changes define index cleanup.
Small datasets may use item-model queries; external search is justified by relevance, aggregation, scale, or query needs.
